notes: Tall shelves (main-left, main-right, leadership) are the standing collection. Stool, O'Reilly, and the stoic/investor display are currently on the desk.

books.title: The Daily Stoic
books.author: Ryan Holiday & Stephen Hanselman
books.summary: A page-a-day companion drawn from Marcus Aurelius, Seneca, and Epictetus. Holiday translates stoic practice into a working discipline: control what you can, meet fortune without drama, and keep a journal honest enough to change you.
books.whyItFits: Jonas talks about judgment, responsibility, and giving people the keys back. A daily stoic practice is the same muscle he asks leaders to use with AI — pause, ask better questions, don’t outsource the hard part.

books.title: Meditations
books.author: Marcus Aurelius
books.summary: The private notes of a Roman emperor writing to himself. Meditations is not a system so much as a repeated return to duty, mortality, and composure under pressure.
books.whyItFits: A consulting lead who teaches executives sits closer to Marcus than to a manifesto: do the work in front of you, stay useful, don’t get drunk on the tool.

books.title: The Intelligent Investor
books.author: Benjamin Graham
books.summary: Graham’s classic on value investing and Mr. Market. Margin of safety, temperament over tips, and the difference between investing and speculation.
books.whyItFits: A decade in alternative investments at Citco, then quant research on the side — this is the foundation text for not confusing a model’s confidence with a thesis.

books.title: Letters from a Stoic
books.author: Seneca
books.summary: Moral letters on time, friendship, wealth, and how to live without being owned by either luxury or fear. Seneca writes like a counselor who has seen power up close.
books.whyItFits: Sits with Meditations and The Daily Stoic on the desk display — a working ethics shelf, not décor.

books.title: Thinking, Fast and Slow
books.author: Daniel Kahneman
books.summary: Kahneman splits cognition into fast intuition and slow analysis, then shows how biases sneak into expert judgment. Required reading if your job is to keep humans from blindly trusting a fluent answer.
books.whyItFits: Jonas’s Concordia teaching keeps returning to professional judgment and blind trust in AI. This is the psychology underneath that warning.

books.title: The Psychology of Money
books.author: Morgan Housel
books.summary: Housel argues that doing well with money is less about spreadsheets than behavior — humility, patience, and room for error. Twenty-odd short stories, one long point.
books.whyItFits: Bridges the Citco years and the tinkerer’s quant notebooks: returns are a lagging indicator of temperament.

books.title: Poor Charlie's Almanack
books.author: Charlie Munger
books.summary: Munger’s talks on multidisciplinary mental models, inversion, and the lollapalooza of getting incentives right. A latticework against one-tool thinking.
books.whyItFits: Jonas’s method for AI work is value, feasibility, and risk — inversion in consulting clothes. Munger is the same instinct with different jokes.

books.title: Range
books.author: David Epstein
books.summary: A case for generalists in a world that over-worships early specialization. Wicked problems reward people who can analogize across fields.
books.whyItFits: Accounting degree, fund-services ladder, self-taught Python at night, now Data & AI. The nontraditional path is the point, not a detour.

books.title: Atomic Habits
books.author: James Clear
books.summary: Clear’s practical system for identity-based habits: make it obvious, attractive, easy, satisfying. Less inspiration, more environment design.
books.whyItFits: Two to three years of nights learning Python and SQL while doing the day job — this is how a career actually turns.

books.title: Python for Data Analysis
books.author: Wes McKinney
books.summary: The pandas book, written by pandas’ creator. Wrangling, time series, aggregation, and the unglamorous work that makes every later model honest.
books.whyItFits: Jonas lists Pandas on his GitHub profile for a reason. This is the craft book under the dashboards, screeners, and trading notebooks.

books.title: Fluent Python
books.author: Luciano Ramalho
books.summary: Python as a language, not a syntax: data model, concurrency, typing, and the patterns that separate scripts from systems you can trust.
books.whyItFits: A self-taught developer who now ships Next.js and agentic tools needs the second book — the one that makes the first decade of code less accidental.

books.title: Designing Data-Intensive Applications
books.author: Martin Kleppmann
books.summary: The field guide to storage, replication, partitioning, and derived data. How serious systems fail, and how to talk about trade-offs without slides.
books.whyItFits: Data platforms and AI-enabled workflows only work if the pipes are real. This is the book you hand a room that wants a model before it wants a schema.

books.title: Hands-On Machine Learning
books.author: Aurélien Géron
books.summary: Scikit-Learn, Keras, and TensorFlow in working order — from training loops to production instincts. A builder’s ML book, not a theorem dump.
books.whyItFits: Matches the curiosity that started when a client was using cloud ML before the hype cycle. How it actually trains, not just what the demo claims.

books.title: Practical Statistics for Data Scientists
books.author: Bruce, Gedeck & Bruce
books.summary: The statistical ideas data work actually uses: sampling, bias, regression, and the ways dashboards lie. Short, pointed, and allergic to cargo-cult metrics.
books.whyItFits: Accounting-trained, risk-aware, allergic to pretty charts with no denominator. Statistics is how he keeps AI projects from becoming theatre.

books.title: Learning Spark
books.author: Damji, Wen, Das & Lee
books.summary: Apache Spark as a data engine: DataFrames, streaming, and the cluster mental model. How to move past the laptop without losing the plot.
books.whyItFits: His portfolio lists big-data work with Spark. This is the O’Reilly that belongs next to pandas, not instead of it.

books.title: High Output Management
books.author: Andrew S. Grove
books.summary: Intel’s CEO on leverage, meetings as work, and the manager as a node in a production process. Still the clearest book on running a team that ships.
books.whyItFits: Team Lead at BDO Digital. Grove is how you scale from doing the analysis to multiplying other people doing it.

books.title: The Hard Thing About Hard Things
books.author: Ben Horowitz
books.summary: Wartime management without the TED-talk glaze: firing friends, peacetime vs wartime CEOs, and telling the truth when the numbers are ugly.
books.whyItFits: Jonas tells leaders to start with the outcome, not the tool. Horowitz is the same honesty applied to people and cash.

books.title: Good to Great
books.author: Jim Collins
books.summary: Collins’s study of companies that made the leap — Level 5 leadership, the Hedgehog Concept, and a culture of discipline. Famous, argued-over, still useful as a prompt.
books.whyItFits: The Growth Pod advising work is hedgehog-shaped: AI strategy for operators who already know their business.

books.title: Extreme Ownership
books.author: Jocko Willink & Leif Babin
books.summary: Former Navy SEALs on the simple, severe idea that if the team failed, you own it. Decentralized command and no bad teams, only bad leaders.
books.whyItFits: Responsibility and accountability are the words Jonas uses for AI. This is that ethic without the lab coat.

books.title: Leaders Eat Last
books.author: Simon Sinek
books.summary: Sinek on Circle of Safety: teams take risks when leaders absorb them first. Culture as a biological trust system, not a poster.
books.whyItFits: “We need to bring our people along with us.” This is the leadership shelf’s human half of the AI transformation speech.

books.title: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team
books.author: Patrick Lencioni
books.summary: Absence of trust, fear of conflict, lack of commitment, avoidance of accountability, inattention to results — told as a fable because the pattern is that common.
books.whyItFits: AI projects stall when IT and the business don’t share a language. Lencioni names the social failure mode.

books.title: Measure What Matters
books.author: John Doerr
books.summary: OKRs as a focusing device: objectives that mean something, key results you can count, and the courage to say no to the rest.
books.whyItFits: Define the three-to-five-year outcome before the model. Doerr is the operating system for that sentence.

books.title: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People
books.author: Stephen R. Covey
books.summary: Begin with the end in mind, put first things first, seek first to understand. A character-ethic book that consulting cultures still quietly run on.
books.whyItFits: Jonas’s dad was a teacher and a coach. Covey is the leadership shelf’s through-line from that house to the client room.

books.title: Radical Candor
books.author: Kim Scott
books.summary: Care personally, challenge directly. Scott’s map of the ruinous empathy and obnoxious aggression that pass for management.
books.whyItFits: Teaching executives and mentoring founders requires the same move: tell the truth without performing toughness.

books.title: Dare to Lead
books.author: Brené Brown
books.summary: Brown on grounded confidence, rumbling with vulnerability, and building courage in organizations that would rather look certain.
books.whyItFits: The people-first half of responsible AI. If the room is anxious, the model will not save the culture.

books.title: A Random Walk Down Wall Street
books.author: Burton G. Malkiel
books.summary: The efficient-market argument in public: index, diversify, ignore the noise. A counterweight to every clever backtest.
books.whyItFits: Quant research is more honest when it has to live next to Malkiel. Not every edge is an edge.

books.title: Fooled by Randomness
books.author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb
books.summary: Taleb’s first strike against surviving by luck and calling it skill. Noise, alternative histories, and the dignity of not narrating every win.
books.whyItFits: Fund-services valuation work and crypto strategy both mint false confidence. Taleb is the seatbelt.

books.title: The Black Swan
books.author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb
books.summary: On the outsized role of rare events and the narrative fallacy that makes them look inevitable afterward. Fragility as a design problem.
books.whyItFits: Risk management is in the original skill list. Black swans are why “it looked good on a spreadsheet” is not a defense.

books.title: Against the Gods
books.author: Peter L. Bernstein
books.summary: The history of risk from dice to derivatives. How probability became a tool, and why that tool still fails at the interesting edges.
books.whyItFits: Accounting plus alternatives — Bernstein is the intellectual history of the job Jonas trained for.

books.title: When Genius Failed
books.author: Roger Lowenstein
books.summary: The rise and 1998 collapse of Long-Term Capital Management. Leverage, models, and the moment the market stopped agreeing with the PhDs.
books.whyItFits: A reminder from the alternatives world: elegant models plus borrowed money is still a story about people.

books.title: Liar's Poker
books.author: Michael Lewis
books.summary: Salomon Brothers as a human comedy of bonds, egos, and the 1980s. The book that made market culture visible to everyone else.
books.whyItFits: Financial services from the inside, written with enough bite to keep a consultant from romanticizing the sell side.

books.title: The Big Short
books.author: Michael Lewis
books.summary: The housing crash through the handful of people who bet against it. Incentives, opacity, and the social cost of not reading the prospectus.
books.whyItFits: Jonas’s north star question — who do you serve, what community impact — is the moral of this book in plainer clothes.

books.title: Flash Boys
books.author: Michael Lewis
books.summary: Speed, fiber, and the fight over whether public markets are still public. A story about infrastructure posing as strategy.
books.whyItFits: HFT-adjacent curiosity and a tinkerer’s respect for pipes. The market is a system, not a vibe.

books.title: The Essays of Warren Buffett
books.author: Warren Buffett (ed. Lawrence Cunningham)
books.summary: The shareholder letters rearranged into a coherent operating manual: moats, managers, and not interrupting compounding.
books.whyItFits: Sits with Graham on the desk. Buffett is what Intelligent Investor looks like after fifty years of practice.

books.title: Security Analysis
books.author: Benjamin Graham & David Dodd
books.summary: The dense original — how to read a balance sheet like it might be lying to you. Partner to The Intelligent Investor, not a sequel.
books.whyItFits: BComm Accounting, then fund services. This is the textbook that still justifies opening the footnotes.

books.title: Superintelligence
books.author: Nick Bostrom
books.summary: Bostrom’s control-problem book: what happens if we succeed at building something smarter than we are, and why “we’ll figure it out later” is not a plan.
books.whyItFits: The lightbulb around generative AI came with a responsibility hangover. This is the long-range version of that hangover.

books.title: Life 3.0
books.author: Max Tegmark
books.summary: Tegmark’s tour of possible AI futures, from near-term jobs to cosmic-scale design. Optimistic enough to keep building, serious enough to set rules.
books.whyItFits: Teaching “Building AI Projects That Deliver” needs a horizon beyond the pilot. Tegmark is the wide shot.

books.title: Human Compatible
books.author: Stuart Russell
books.summary: Russell’s case for AI that remains uncertain about human preferences instead of optimizing a proxy into the ground. Alignment as engineering.
books.whyItFits: “Does this make sense? Does it fit my objective? What am I missing?” — the same questions, aimed at the machine.

books.title: Weapons of Math Destruction
books.author: Cathy O'Neil
books.summary: How scoring systems punish the poor, launder bias, and call it objective. A necessary cold shower for anyone selling models to institutions.
books.whyItFits: If it damages trust, it is not a good idea. O’Neil is the worked example.

books.title: The Book of Why
books.author: Judea Pearl & Dana Mackenzie
books.summary: Causal diagrams for people who are tired of correlation theatre. Interventions, counterfactuals, and why prediction is not explanation.
books.whyItFits: Data strategy that starts with the business objective is a causal claim. Pearl is how you stop pretending a dashboard is a why.

books.title: Prediction Machines
books.author: Agrawal, Gans & Goldfarb
books.summary: AI as a drop in the cost of prediction, which makes judgment and data more valuable, not less. An economist’s map of the same shift Jonas teaches.
books.whyItFits: This is the faculty-lounge version of “technology decisions come after the business objective.”

books.title: Competing in the Age of AI
books.author: Iansiti & Lakhani
books.summary: How AI-centric firms rebuild the operating model, not just the org chart. Scale, scope, learning — and the mess of actually doing it.
books.whyItFits: BDO clients don’t need a lab. They need the operating model conversation this book names.

books.title: The Pragmatic Programmer
books.author: Andrew Hunt & David Thomas
books.summary: Craft habits for people who write software for a living: orthogonality, tracer bullets, and not setting the building on fire with cleverness.
books.whyItFits: Self-taught, still shipping. The Pragmatic Programmer is the missing CS department.

books.title: Deep Work
books.author: Cal Newport
books.summary: Newport’s argument that focused cognitive work is both rare and valuable, and that you have to defend it like a calendar, not a mood.
books.whyItFits: Nights of Python after a full Citco day only work if someone protects the hours. This is that defense.

books.title: Sapiens
books.author: Yuval Noah Harari
books.summary: A wide history of how shared fictions — money, law, gods, limited companies — let strangers cooperate. Sweeping, arguable, and hard to unread.
books.whyItFits: The community-impact question sits on a longer timeline than a sprint. Harari is the long shelf.
